title: Graphs, Degrees and the Handshake Lemma
quickIdea: A graph is dots and lines; the degrees of its vertices add to twice the number of lines, and that one identity carries most of the counting questions in this topic.
remember: A simple graph has no loop and no repeated edge between the same pair; a multigraph may have both, and a loop adds 2 to the degree of its vertex.
Handshake lemma: the degrees of all vertices sum to 2|E|, so the number of odd-degree vertices is always even.
A simple graph on n vertices has at most n(n-1)/2 edges, reached only by the complete graph K_n, in which every vertex has degree n-1.
The complement of G has the same vertices and an edge exactly where G has none, so |E(G)| + |E(complement of G)| = n(n-1)/2.
A walk may repeat vertices and edges, a trail repeats no edge, a path repeats no vertex, and a cycle is a closed path of length at least 3.
A k-regular graph on n vertices has nk/2 edges, so nk must be even before such a graph can exist.

example.prompt: A simple graph has degree sequence 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2. How many edges does it have, and how many of its vertices have odd degree?
example.work: The degrees sum to 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 14, and the handshake lemma says the sum is 2|E|, so |E| = 7. The odd degrees are the two 3s, so exactly 2 vertices have odd degree, which is an even count as the lemma requires.

gateAngle: GATE uses this as the first step of counting questions: the maximum number of edges in a simple graph on n vertices with k components, C(n-k+1, 2), and whether a degree sequence can be realised. Both are one-line consequences of the handshake lemma and the edge bound.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A simple graph on 8 vertices has 25 edges. What is the minimum number of edges in its complement?
variations.why: The complement's edge count is forced by the total n(n-1)/2, not by the structure of G.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Can a simple graph have exactly five vertices of odd degree?
variations.answer: No. Odd-degree vertices come in pairs, so their number is always even.
variations.why: The degree sum is 2|E|, an even number, and only the odd degrees contribute to its parity.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: Does a 3-regular graph on 7 vertices exist?
variations.answer: No. 3 x 7 = 21 is odd, so no graph, not even a multigraph, is 3-regular on 7 vertices.
variations.why: A k-regular graph on n vertices has nk/2 edges, which must be a whole number.

trap.what: Accepting a degree sequence as realisable because its sum is even.
trap.why: An even sum is necessary but not sufficient. The sequence 3, 3, 3, 1 sums to 10 and still cannot be drawn: the three vertices of degree 3 would each need every other vertex as a neighbour, which forces degree 3 on the last vertex.
trap.counterexample: The sequence 3, 3, 3, 1 on 4 vertices is not graphic, although its sum is even.

check.question: Is 6, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 the degree sequence of a simple graph on 7 vertices?
check.answer: No. The sum is 27, which is odd, so no graph has this sequence.
check.explanation: The handshake lemma forbids it outright: 27 is not 2|E| for any whole number |E|. A second reason points the same way, because a vertex of degree 6 in a 7-vertex simple graph is adjacent to all six others, so the other six vertices all have degree at least 1 and one of them would need degree 7.
